asDecan.p: Every sign is cut into three ten-degree slices called decans, each with a planet and a small card. Your Sun is in the last of Gemini's, between 20 and 29 degrees, and in the old Chaldean order that slice belongs to the Sun itself. The Sun has no special dignity in Gemini. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, so it takes its tone from Mercury, who rules the sign. The Eight of Swords, Jupiter's slice, weighs every option and can't settle on one. The Nine, Mars's, is the one lying awake at three in the morning. By the Ten the thinking has run all the way out, and the Sun shows the whole thing plainly, ending included. The picture looks grim, I know. Look along the horizon, though, at the strip of gold. The Lovers is your Sun card and this is the finer grain inside it, close enough to Cancer that home pulls on it more than you'd guess.

Whatever's going on, you want to know how it ends. A friend mentions their landlord's put the rent up, and by the time the coffee's finished you've walked them through the whole thing, the letter they should send, what happens if he says no, where they'd move and how long the commute would be. In a work meeting you're the one asking what the last step is while everyone else is still on slide three. Your sister takes a day to answer a message and you've already worked out why, start to finish, before dinner. And then, which is the part people miss, you're done with it. Loose ends bother you far more than bad news does. A free Saturday usually goes on tying them off, returning the parcel, answering the email you've been avoiding, ringing your mum back.

You can say a thing is over, mean it, and have people believe you. A project at work has been limping along for eight months, everyone's still putting hours in because nobody wants to be the one, and you're the one who says in the meeting that it isn't going to work and explains why. It lands because you've clearly thought it all the way through. The same happens with friends. Someone rings you at eleven at night halfway through a break-up and you let them tell you the whole thing, the worst version, every bit of it. Somewhere near the end they hear themselves and feel lighter, because the worst bit has been said out loud and it turns out they can stand it. You also get up quickly after your own setbacks, quicker than most, and that steadies the people around you.

Where it goes wrong is calling time too early. You get to the end of a story so fast that you sometimes decide something's finished when it only needed one hard conversation. A flatmate leaves the kitchen in a state twice and in your head the arrangement's already over, you've looked at other flats, and they haven't a clue anything's wrong. A job has one bad quarter and there's a resignation letter sitting in your notes app. Then there's the storytelling. You tell a good story, you're a Gemini, and bad things make the best stories, so the disaster gets told at dinner and told again and gets a little bigger each time. After a while you're more attached to the version where it all went wrong than to what happened, and the people who were there start to notice the two don't quite match.

When something really goes wrong, a redundancy, a friend falling out with you, a parent going into hospital, the first thing you do is talk. You ring three people in one evening and tell each of them the whole thing, and every time it gets clearer and a bit worse. You're up late looking things up, the worst outcome, then the second worst. About a week later there's usually a strange calm. You've decided it's the end of something and you've already started on what comes next, which can look very sudden from outside. The cost lands on whoever's still upset. Your partner is still grieving the old plan while you're on to the new one, and they can feel left behind. What actually helps is sleep, a proper meal at home, and letting one person be sad about it with you for longer than feels useful.

You need a conversation to finish. An argument left hanging overnight is close to unbearable, so you'll follow your partner from room to room at midnight trying to get to the end of it, and someone who needs to go quiet and think it over can find that exhausting. The Cancer side of these degrees shows up at home. You like having someone there at the end of the day, dinner at the table, the same side of the bed, and whoever gets to see that gets a very loyal person. When a relationship does end you tend to end it properly. No getting back together three times, no hovering around each other's lives online. You've said why and you go. Exes sometimes find that cold. Usually it means you did most of the grieving while it was still going, quietly, in your own head.

The Lovers as your Sun card is about choosing, and this slice is good at the choice nobody else wants to make. You tend to do well where the job is finishing things or explaining bad news clearly. Editing, where most of the work is cutting. Project close-outs and post-mortems. Crisis communications, turnaround work, insolvency, being the manager sent in to wind a team down decently. Journalism, especially anything with a hard deadline and a final version. You're very good at the last ten per cent of a job, the stretch where everything has to be pulled together and said plainly. The risk is getting known as the person who kills things and being handed only the grim jobs. Tell your manager you'd like to start something as well, and take the next new project when it's offered, even a small one.

At twenty this decan often looks like a lot of dramatic endings. Friendships finished over one bad night, a course dropped in week three, a break-up announced to the whole group before the other person has quite caught up. Everything feels final because you can see where it's heading so quickly. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have been wrong about an ending or two, and it softens them. They still see the end of the road early, and they're more willing to walk a bit further before deciding. Most have a rough year or two behind them by then, and know they got up again. The fifties tend to bring the Cancer side forward, the house, the family, the friends who stuck around. A lot of them end up the calm one in the hospital corridor, saying the plain thing that needs saying and staying on to help with the washing-up.

When you notice you've already written the ending, the flatmate you've decided to move out on, the friend you've decided has gone off you, the job you're halfway out of in your head, ask the person involved one plain question before you do anything. 'Is something up?' is often enough. The real answer is usually duller than the one you'd worked out, and occasionally it's worse. Give them a day to reply properly, and keep your version to yourself while you wait.
